summary: Analog Experience is an interactive website that compares five Earth locations with Mars. Users select a site on an interactive planet and see its environmental data, a side-by-side comparison with Mars, and its similarities and differences.
details:
What it does and how it works.

The site opens with a definition of a terrestrial analog site and then shows an interactive globe with a marker for each of the five locations. Users can zoom into a site or explore freely, with a “Global View” option to return. For each location, three sections are available: Information (environmental data and a scientific summary), Comparison (Earth vs. Mars parameters in a table), and Similarities (matching and differing characteristics). We also wrote an accompanying report that explains each site’s scientific value, potential applications, and limitations.

Benefits and intended impact.

The project makes analog-site selection easier to understand for students, researchers, and the public. Instead of calling a site “Mars-like,” it shows which parameters match and which do not, and what research each site suits.

Tools and technologies.

We built the site with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, designed the comparison tables in HTML/CSS (prototyped on CodePen), and published it on GitHub Pages. Data came from NASA POWER (temperature, precipitation, humidity, wind, pressure, solar energy), ISRIC SoilGrids (soil), the Meteoritical Society Bulletin, Norwegian Polar Institute, and peer-reviewed papers on pyroxenes, Antarctic microbial diversity, and the Azzel-Matti structure. We used AI assistance for drafting, corrections and organizing content, and the team reviewed it.

Creativity.

The experience turns raw environmental tables into an explorable planet-based interface with a custom logo and identity. It also treats analogs honestly: each site is presented as a partial analog, with explicit limitations rather than overstated similarity. Proposing Cuitzeo and Chachalacas as process and operational analogs is an original angle.

Factors considered.

Humidity, precipitation, wind, solar energy, minerals, soil, and weather events) and noted differences that data alone cannot capture, such as gravity, radiation, biological activity, and human influence. We also stressed that shared mineral names don’t mean equal composition and that similar wind speeds don’t imply the same sand transport at Mars’s 636 Pa pressure. Finally, we clarified that Cuitzeo and Chachalacas are research proposals, not NASA-validated test sites.

Link to our report: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Lix6q7YyjIOFZrVhIM39z-wtY9BzUbLFAmMJ8rmgJ2w/edit?usp=sharing
